paragraphs: I have just observed that in democratic ages monuments of the arts tend to become more numerous and less important. I now hasten to point out the exception to this rule. In a democratic community individuals are very powerless, but the State, which represents them all and holds them all in its grasp, is very powerful. Nowhere do citizens appear so insignificant as in a democratic nation. Nowhere does the nation itself appear greater, or the mind more easily take in a broad general view of it. In democratic communities the imagination shrinks when men consider themselves, and expands without limit when they think of the State. This is why the same men who live on a small scale in narrow dwellings often aspire to gigantic splendor in building their public monuments.

The Americans marked out the boundary of an immense city on the site they intended for their capital. Up to now it is hardly more densely populated than Pontoise, though according to them it will one day hold a million inhabitants. They have already uprooted trees for ten miles around, so that they would not get in the way of the future citizens of this imaginary metropolis. They have built a magnificent palace for Congress in the center of the city and given it the pompous name of the Capitol. The several States of the Union are every day planning and building prodigious undertakings that would astonish the engineers of the great European nations. Thus democracy not only leads men to a vast number of unimportant productions; it also leads them to raise some monuments on the largest scale. But between these two extremes there is a blank. A few scattered remains of enormous buildings can therefore teach us nothing about the social condition and the institutions of the people who raised them. I may add, though the remark takes me outside my subject, that they do not tell us any more about that people’s greatness, its civilization, or its real prosperity. Whenever a power of any kind is able to make a whole people cooperate in a single undertaking, that power, with a little knowledge and a great deal of time, will manage to obtain something enormous from the cooperation of so many efforts. But this does not lead to the conclusion that the people was very happy, very educated, or even very strong.

When the Spaniards reached the City of Mexico, they found it full of magnificent temples and vast palaces. That did not stop Cortes from conquering the Mexican Empire with 600 foot soldiers and sixteen horses. Had the Romans understood the laws of hydraulics better, they would not have built all the aqueducts whose remains surround their ruined cities, and they would have put their power and wealth to better use. Had they invented the steam engine, perhaps they would not have stretched those long artificial roads, the so-called Roman roads, out to the far edges of their empire. These works are at once splendid memorials of their ignorance and of their greatness. A people that left behind no other trace of its passage than a few lead pipes in the ground and a few iron rods on the surface might have been more truly the master of nature than the Romans were.
